headline: Senior AI Engineer | Agentic AI | Intelligent Automation 🤖| AGI & AI Agents enthusiastic | Certified AAP
text:
This is a good starting point if you're trying to make sense of AI agents.

There’s a lot of talk about agent frameworks right now, but at the core, most of them build on the same set of ideas.

This cheat sheet gives a simple overview of the key building blocks—from LLMs to orchestration to protocols. Useful whether you’re exploring agent tooling, building internal automations, or just trying to understand the space better.

🔍 What is an AI agent?

Think of an AI agent like a smart personal assistant:

It doesn't just answer questions (like a chatbot), but can plan your day, book meetings, send emails, and make decisions based on context—automatically.

🧠 Language Model (LM)

This is the brain of the assistant. It reads your message and decides what needs to be done. But on its own, it can't actually do things like booking a ride.

🛠️ Tools

These are like the apps your assistant uses—Google Calendar, Uber, Email, etc. The agent accesses these through APIs and functions to take action in the real world.

🎯 Orchestration Layer

This is the task manager—it decides the order of steps, how to reason through complex tasks, and when to use which tool. It’s the difference between a smart assistant and one that panics with multitasking.

🌐 Agentic Protocols

These are like standard rules or networks that let assistants work across platforms (like coordinating between Slack, GitHub, and Email), and maintain memory over time.

🧱 Building AI Agents

There’s no single way to build an agent:

Some use a single smart prompt

Others rely on low-code platforms

Some build custom, end-to-end systems


The cheat sheet maps out these trade-offs clearly.

#aiagents #cheatsheet

text:
𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲 asked these SQL questions in a Data Engineering interview (𝟯+ 𝗬𝗢𝗘)
CTC → 𝟯𝟬–𝟰𝟬 𝗟𝗣𝗔 (Difficulty level = Advanced)

1.⁠ ⁠Calculate daily user retention for a 30-day cohort window.
2.⁠ ⁠Retrieve the latest 3 events per user using window functions.
3.⁠ ⁠Detect out-of-order events in time-series logs using timestamps.
4.⁠ ⁠Backfill missing dates in a partitioned dataset using calendar table.
5.⁠ ⁠Compute rolling 7-day distinct active users per platform.
6.⁠ ⁠Identify users with no activity in the last 30 days (churn analysis).
7.⁠ ⁠Perform multi-level aggregation (category → subcategory → product).
8.⁠ ⁠Compare current vs previous month revenue per region.
9.⁠ ⁠Join fact and dimension tables with SCD Type 2 handling.
10.⁠ ⁠Detect schema drift between raw and curated layers via metadata.
11.⁠ ⁠Calculate 95th percentile of transaction amounts by user.
12.⁠ ⁠Fetch top 3 categories contributing to 80% of total revenue.
13.⁠ ⁠Identify seasonal patterns in monthly product sales.
14.⁠ ⁠Use broadcast join hints to optimize small dimension lookups.
15.⁠ ⁠Flag revenue anomalies using z-score or standard deviation.
16.⁠ ⁠Remove duplicates using ROW_NUMBER on ingestion timestamp.
17.⁠ ⁠Calculate session time from login-logout events.
18.⁠ ⁠Compare revenue growth across last 3 quarters per product line.
19.⁠ ⁠Identify users who upgraded to premium but never used the features.
20.⁠ ⁠Track update frequency on records in an SCD Type 2 table.
